title: GIL and Subinterpreter Experiments + Request Parse Benchmarks
content:
Summary:

This is a scratchpad + experiment log for CPU-side investigation into repeated request-parse and Python GIL contention during peak serving. Goal: identify low-effort mitigations we can apply in the next sprint (1–2 weeks) to reduce p95 latency and free up vCPU headroom on customers using single-node Dedicated pools.

Why this matters:
- We see sustained CPU utilization on small requests (short prompts) that is disproportionate to model inference time.
- Tokenization + request parsing + short-lived Python callbacks are a dominant percent of end-to-end p50 when model latency is low (fast quantized models).

What we tried (high level):
1) Microbench tokenization: compare HuggingFace tokenizers (rust) via tokenizers bindings vs byte-level Python split + regex.
2) Request body parsing: measure Starlette/FastAPI overhead for small JSON convos; test lower-level raw parsing (uvicorn loop + manual json.loads) vs standard dependency injection.
3) Threadpool sizing & sync-to-async transitions: measure blocking calls that run on default ThreadPoolExecutor and cause main loop wakeups.
4) GIL mitigation experiments: isolate long-running CPU-bound logic into subinterpreters (py3.11 trial build) and into small C extension where feasible.

Setup details:
- Test harness: 48-core c6i.12xlarge equivalent, 64GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15.
- Python: 3.11.6 (baseline), custom build with --with-pydebug for subinterp tests.
- Framework: Uvicorn 0.20.0 + FastAPI; uvloop on by default except where noted.
- Clients: wrk2 for constant-QPS runs and a custom asyncio harness to generate 1–500 concurrent short requests (avg 80–120B payload).
- Profilers: py-spy (flamegraphs), linux perf + FlameGraph scripts, eBPF via tracee/Tracee-extras for syscalls.

Key microbench results (median of 5 runs):
- Baseline (python split regex tokenization, FastAPI body parsing): p50=6.2ms, p95=24.6ms at 200 QPS, CPU 62% per core on average.
- Rust tokenizers binding (tokenizers 0.13 via pip): p50=4.8ms, p95=16.4ms. Tokenization CPU dropped ~35%.
- Manual raw parsing (uvicorn.receive -> json.loads without FastAPI deps): p50=5.6ms, p95=15.2ms. Removes ~40–60µs per request from hot path (throughput increased ~8% at 200 QPS).
- Moving small sync work to a dedicated ProcessPool (multiprocessing with shared mem mmap): p50=5.1ms, p95=18.0ms but added jitter for GC cycles.
- Subinterpreter experiment (unstable): successful isolation of an expensive tokenizer-only worker into an interpreter per core reduced cross-request GIL contention; measured p95=13.9ms but build was fragile and had memory regressions.

Observations from profiles:
- A large fraction (~30–45%) of CPU time for short-requests is in Python bytecode: frame handling, json loads, and small helper functions in request model validation (pydantic).
- Tokenization implemented in pure Python (legacy path) is a major hotpath — switching to rust-backed tokenizers drops CPU significantly.
- ThreadPoolExecutor blocking bursts cause the main event loop threads to contend on the GIL when workers return, visible as 'GIL wait' stacks in py-spy.
- Garbage collection pauses are visible at ~4–5s intervals during steady runs with ephemeral objects; forcing generational tuning (PYTHONMALLOC, disable debug alloc) reduced tail latency.

Actionable recommendations (prioritized):
1) Replace legacy Python tokenizer with rust-tokenizers bindings on the default code path (low-risk, big win). Track memory increase on tokenizers v0.13.
2) Remove expensive FastAPI dependency injection for the hot /v1/generate route: implement a minimal raw-body handler that performs a single json.loads and a lightweight validation (handwritten checks) — this shaves ~40–100µs per request.
3) Move blocking external calls (sync DB / metrics) off the default ThreadPoolExecutor into a dedicated small pool to avoid starving the loop. Use aiomultiprocess for heavy CPU tasks.
4) Tune GC: set PYTHONMALLOC=malloc in dedicated worker images and experiment with GC thresholds (via gc.set_threshold) in a canary.
5) Long term: investigate subinterpreters for isolating third-party extensions (PEP 554/684) but treat as experimental. Prefer C-extensions for microcritical paths if we can ship them within 3 sprints.

Notes on threadpools and GIL observed patterns:
- Default executor size (min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4)) ends up with more threads than useful for short blocking I/O. When many tasks submit small CPU work to the pool, the returning worker threads attempt to grab the GIL causing short global pauses.
- Experiment: setting ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) in the server reduces context switching and slightly improves p95 at low concurrency but throttles throughput at high QPS. Conclusion: expose a config knob and tune per-customer profile.

Spike patches (links and short description):
- PR 2483: switch default tokenizer to tokenizers rust binding; includes a compatibility shim for old token offsets. (see linked_artifacts)
- Branch gil-subinterp-experiment: prototype using interp_new APIs to create interpreters per worker process. Not for prod.

Open questions / risks:
- Memory profile of rust tokenizers under long-running workloads — observed a small steady-state increase in RSS (~40MB) per worker compared to Python tokenizer. Need longer soak tests.
- Pydantic validation cost vs safety tradeoff: can we relax full model parsing on hot paths? Need product/contract review.
- Subinterpreters are not yet fully supported by some C-extensions; may break third-party libs used by customers.

Next steps / short term plan (2 weeks):
- Ship tokenizer switch as an opt-in feature flag for Dedicated customers; monitor CPU and RSS for 2 weeks (owner: Marcus).
- Implement minimal raw-body handler for /v1/generate behind a feature flag; run A/B test on internal canary (owner: Diego).
- Add configuration knobs for ThreadPoolExecutor size exposed at container start (owner: Hannah).

Raw commands used (for reproducibility):
- wrk2: wrk -t12 -c200 -d60s -R200 -s scripts/post-short.lua http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/generate
- py-spy record: py-spy record -o flame.svg --pid $(pgrep -f uvicorn) --native --rate 1000 --duration 30
- perf: sudo perf record -F 999 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30 && sudo perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./flamegraph.pl > perf.svg

Appendix: quick perf tips learned:
- uvloop + httptools combo consistently reduces syscall counts compared to older uvicorn combos. Always ensure uvloop is enabled in customer images.
- For JSON-heavy small payloads, ujson shows wins but sometimes produces slightly different float formatting; check inputs/outputs.

If you review this and want me to split into separate PRs (tokenizer / handler / threadpool), I can produce three clean RFC snippets and a canary run plan.

Notes to self: keep a copy of the long-running memory traces and eBPF syscall logs in the /tmp/serving-perf-soak-2026-02.

-- Ava
